During those long years he had made himself—in a word—a half a hand of friendly Chinese. They learned to love him because they realized he was true, and felt constrained by that love which was shed abroad. If, on arriving at a town, he went to the market-place and cried out with a loud voice, "Tin ming! Jin ming!" which means "Save life!" As a result, great crowds of people came running from every direction. The object was not that any danger was at hand; but where there seemed to be no danger. When the excitement had somewhat quieted, he said, "Friends, I did not call because I wanted you to save my life, but because I want you to know that the Living God wishes to save your lives for eternity, for ever and ever."

Mr. Pierce was a man much given to Bible study and prayer, rising often at 4 o'clock to read the Bible and to pray. He believed that the strength for day's work was done often reading God's Word far into the night. He was earnest in all that he did. A childhood incident illustrates this attitude. They were requiring a work at the hay field. When darkness came on, he suggested that they stop. His father frowned, and said to his father, "I'll go down if you will hold the rope." The same earnest and compelling faith was characteristic of his attitude toward life.

In his preaching trips he traveled the country: on sail-boat, on donkey-back, or by wheelbarrow. On a journey, once, to China, some thirty or forty miles from Yangchow, he met a servant of the people, traveling with a foreign face. A Chinese gentleman fell to looking at him and decided to converse with that servant. He looked not on the outward form but reproached the foreigners of his condition. If Mr. Pierce needed rest, he would take a short sleep, and he would improvise a bed from a table or some planks placed across chairs. On one occasion, a Bible-woman was visiting a place at the same time and seeing the condition in which he slept, she reported to some of the Chinese Christian women who love ease and comfort.
